Methods and recorded history

The broader Senate/House model is a dated research snapshot. The original Senate polling study keeps its own daily captures and scoring record. This shared interface preserves both studies and their source dates.

Two-chamber research: historical checks

Expanding-cycle fits hold out 2020, 2022 and 2024, each with at least four earlier cycles. These are selected D/R contests, not complete chamber-control backtests. Historical publication lags are reconstructed proxies. Three correlated elections do not establish calibrated control odds or an edge.

Original polling v1 on exactly matched historical Senate races

Earlier cycles only, under unchanged v1 code. The original pilot uses its own probability-clipping convention.

Full historical population and exclusions
Stan sampling diagnostics

Four chains; 1,000 warmup and retained draws per chain; adapt_delta 0.99. Publication requires zero divergences and depth hits, R-hat ≤ 1.01, bulk/tail ESS ≥ 400 and the energy check.

Original recorded Senate polling study

Latest eligible poll per firm within 45 days, equal firm weights, with shared election error and race-specific uncertainty. Missing, stale and multiparty races remain excluded. It does not provide full Senate-control odds. Historical validation did not establish better winner prediction than the fixed three-point polling baseline.

Original validation and uncertainty

Assumptions and sources

House fundamentals use earlier presidential votes re-tabulated onto the target election’s district maps, with national generic-ballot polling. The model estimates chamber-specific effects, correlated national cycle errors, shared state errors and separate race noise. It does not include House district polls, candidate or incumbency effects. Modelled races approximate D/R outcomes; minor-party wins are not simulated.

Current candidate lists are reported fields, not certified ballot captures. New independent winners are not assigned to a caucus. Senate arithmetic starts with 34 Democratic-aligned and 31 Republican holdovers. A 50–50 Senate is not a Democratic majority. Historical 2024 Senate polls use an Electoral-Vote supplement, a disclosed source change from 538.
